consensus_summary: All three blind responses converge on the same core: 'heart of the earth' in Matthew 12:40 refers to Jesus's burial in the grave/tomb, commonly extended to the realm of the dead (Sheol/Hades) via the descent tradition, framed by the Jonah typology. The Jerusalem reading appears only as an explicitly minority/rare alternative (Responses A and B), advanced mainly to fix the three-days-and-nights chronology.
book_summary: The book identifies 'heart of the earth' as Jerusalem, the navel/heart of the land, citing Ezekiel 5:5 and 38:12 (Jerusalem set 'in the midst of the nations' / dwelling 'in the midst of the land'). It expressly flags the grave/Hades reading as merely the 'commonly taught' view it departs from.
consensus_core_identification: The grave/tomb of Jesus (his interval among the dead between death and resurrection), often widened to Sheol/Hades.
book_core_identification: The city of Jerusalem as the geographic-covenantal center ('navel/heart') of the land, so the three days and nights are located in Jerusalem rather than in the tomb or underworld.
boundary_disagreement: Under the book's reading, the period signified would plausibly begin with Jesus's custody in Jerusalem (arrest/trial) rather than with burial, reclassifying which hours count toward the 'three days and three nights.' The consensus reading confines the referent to entombment/the state of death.
material_contradiction: 'Heart of the earth' cannot simultaneously mean the grave/realm of the dead and the city of Jerusalem in the same sense of Matthew 12:40. The book's common-view note explicitly sets its identification against the grave/Hades reading, so accepting the book requires rejecting the consensus's central referent, not merely adjusting its boundary.
rationale: The consensus core is the tomb/Sheol; the book's core is Jerusalem-as-center-of-the-land. These are different referents (a burial place or death-state vs. a city), and the book signals replacement by labeling the grave/Hades view as merely 'commonly taught.' Although Responses A and B list the Jerusalem reading, they classify it as a minority/rare alternative, so the book is not NOVEL — its identification is recognizable — but it contradicts the primary consensus identification rather than refining it. This matches DIVERGENT: a replaced central referent, even though the two readings overlap on the surrounding facts (Jonah typology, death-and-resurrection context).
strongest_objection: One could argue REFINED: both readings still concern where/when Jesus spent the sign-of-Jonah interval, and the Jerusalem reading is already catalogued within the consensus responses as a known alternative, so the book merely relocates the boundary of the same prophetic period rather than abandoning the referent. But the referent itself (grave/underworld vs. city) is what changes, and the book's note frames it as rejection of the common identification, which fits DIVERGENT better than boundary refinement.
